title: Chapter XL

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth tells Jane of Darcy's proposal and of Wickham's true character. Jane is distressed for both men. The sisters agree not to expose Wickham publicly, since he is leaving soon. Elizabeth keeps back Darcy's part in separating Jane and Bingley.

vocabulary.context: Here was knowledge in which no one could partake; and she was sensible that nothing less than a perfect understanding between the parties could justify her in throwing off this last incumbrance of mystery.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “incumbrance”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ance (Latin -antia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “There certainly was some great mismanagement in the education of those two young men.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mismanagement”: mis- (Old English mis-, "wrongly") + man (Latin manus, "hand") + -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: He is now perhaps sorry for what he has done, and anxious to reestablish a character.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “reestablish”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To make quiet or put at rest
vocabulary.context: The tumult of Elizabeth’s mind was allayed by this conversation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “allay”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To cause to be no longer deceived
vocabulary.context: On the contrary every particular relative to his sister, was meant to be kept as much as possible to myself; and if I endeavour to undeceive people as to the rest of his conduct, who will believe me?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “undeceive”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + -ive (Latin -ivus, "tending to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Darcy, for now they do appear wholly undeserved.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “undeserve”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To wrest from an unwilling person by physical force, menace, duress, torture, or any undue or illegal exercise of…
vocabulary.context: It was some time, however, before a smile could be extorted from Jane.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “extort”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Well, if they can be easy with an estate that is not lawfully their own, so much the better.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “lawful”: -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To trip in walking or in moving in any way with the legs
vocabulary.context: One may be continually abusive without saying anything just; but one cannot be always laughing at a man without now and then stumbling on something witty.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “stumble”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Changing in place, position, or direction
vocabulary.context: There is but such a quantity of merit between them; just enough to make one good sort of man; and of late it has been shifting about pretty much.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “shifting”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Damaging a man's reputation without proof could bring social consequences.

significance: The decision to stay silent sets up the elopement crisis.
discussionQuestions: Was it right to keep Wickham's character secret?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with women's limited choices?

items.prompt: What does Elizabeth hold back from Jane?
options: Darcy's role in separating her from Bingley

items.prompt: What theme does the silence raise?

options: To make quiet or put at rest

items.prompt: In the line ““There certainly was some great mismanagement in the education of those two young men.”, what does “mismanagement” most nearly mean?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XL,” how does Austen show keeping secrets? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XL develops the idea of keeping secrets. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XL to complicate the reader's understanding of keeping secrets. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XL within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of keeping secrets responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XL as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of keeping secrets. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: “This will not do,” said Elizabeth. “You never will be able to make both of them good for anything. Take your choice, but you must be satisfied with only one. There is but such a quantity of merit between them; just enough to make one good sort of man; and of late it has been shifting about pretty much. segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Was it right to keep Wickham's character secret? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are incumbrance, mismanagement, reestablish, allayed, undeceive. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Here was knowledge in which no one could partake; and she was sensible that nothing less than a perfect understanding between the parties could justify her in throwing off this last incumbrance of mystery.” Webster's says: A burdensome and troublesome load. Now the word history: “incumbrance”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ance (Latin -antia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “mismanagement”: mis- (Old English mis-, "wrongly") + man (Latin manus, "hand") + -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “reestablish”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Damaging a man's reputation without proof could bring social consequences. Why does this chapter matter? The decision to stay silent sets up the elopement crisis. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to keeping secrets.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Foreshadowing, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “This will not do,” said Elizabeth. “You never will be able to make both of them good for anything. Take your choice, but you must be satisfied with only one. There is but such a quantity of merit between them; just enough to make one good sort of man; and of late it has been shifting about pretty much. For my part, I am inclined to believe it all Mr. Darcy’s, but you shall do as you choose.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Foreshadowing, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XL,” how does Austen show keeping secrets? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about keeping secrets, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes keeping secrets. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
